passage: Chaitanya had wanted to sell his mother's sabudana vada for a year, and for a year he had known it would flop. On a scrap of paper in his Nagpur flat he wrote: 'Nobody buys. 85% sure.' His friend Lalit read it over his shoulder. 'Eighty-five, not a hundred? So there's room.' That Sunday Chaitanya carried just thirty vadas to the colony's weekend market on a borrowed folding table. By noon nineteen were gone, and an aunty asked if he came every week. At home he added a line under the first: 'Got: 19 of 30 sold. Forecast too gloomy.' Lalit tapped the paper. 'Keep this. Next time you're eighty-five percent sure, look at it first.' Chaitanya pinned it above his desk, next to a fresh blank slip.

qa.q: How many vadas were gone by noon?
qa.a: By noon nineteen of the thirty vadas were gone.

qa.q: Why had Chaitanya held back for a whole year?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt so sure the vadas would flop that the forecast felt like knowledge, and not trying spared him the sting of watching nobody buy.

qa.q: Which step made the experiment safe enough to try?
qa.a: Taking only thirty vadas on a borrowed table kept the cost small, so even a flop would have been bearable and any result would still teach him something.

qa.q: What would change if Chaitanya's slip had said 'Got: 3 sold'?
qa.a: It would still be useful: Chaitanya could adjust the price or place, and over time the slips would show which forecasts are accurate rather than just gloomy.

grounding: Shows an adult rating his confidence that a small food venture will fail, testing a small version, and writing what happened next to the forecast.

'The green notebook again?' Binita put two cups of butter tea on the table.
'Mm. Tomorrow I ask Ma'am for the team-lead training.'
'And?'
'Prediction: she says I'm not ready. Confidence: eighty percent.'
Binita leaned over. 'Show me the old pages.'
Tenzin flipped back. 'March: landlord refuses to fix the geyser, ninety percent. Got: fixed in two days. June: nobody comes to my momo-making class, seventy-five percent. Got: six people.'
'So how many of your eighty-percent disasters actually happened?'
Tenzin counted. 'Two out of nine.'
'Then maybe write sixty.'
He crossed out eighty and wrote sixty, then laughed. 'Still gloomy.'
'Kinder, though.'
The next evening he came in and went straight for the notebook. 'Got: let's try you on one project first. Not a no.'

qa.q: How many of Tenzin's eighty-percent disasters actually happened?
qa.a: Two out of nine actually happened.

qa.q: Why does Tenzin laugh and say 'Still gloomy' after changing the number?
qa.a: Tenzin can see from his own record that the forecasts run too dark, and feels a little amused and relieved that even sixty percent is on the pessimistic side.

qa.q: What makes the green notebook useful over time?
qa.a: Writing each prediction with a confidence number and then the real result shows Tenzin a pattern, so later forecasts become more accurate and less harsh.

qa.q: How might Binita see the notebook habit?
qa.a: Binita seems to see it as a gentle tool that lets Tenzin argue with fear using his own evidence, which is why Binita asks for the old pages instead of just saying 'don't worry'.

passage: Last year, when Deepika asked me to read a poem at the library's open evening, I said no before she finished the sentence. I knew my hands would shake and the room would go politely silent. Afterwards I felt silly, so I tried something. In my phone notes I wrote: 'Reading aloud to strangers = disaster. 95% sure.' Then I read one short poem to four people at Deepika's book circle. Not the open evening, just the circle. My hands did shake. Nobody noticed, or they were kind about it. I wrote: 'Got: shaky hands, two people asked the poem's name.' I've done it eleven times now. My number has dropped to forty, and the notes are a strange comfort: a list of times I, Trisha, was wrong about myself in a good way.

qa.q: How many people did Trisha read to at the book circle?
qa.a: Trisha read one short poem to four people.

qa.q: Why does Trisha call the notes 'a strange comfort'?
qa.a: The notes show, in plain facts, how often the fear was wrong, which reassures Trisha in a way that being told 'you'll be fine' never could 🙂.

qa.q: Why was the book circle a good first step?
qa.a: It was a small, low-risk version of the open evening, so Trisha could compare the ninety-five percent forecast with a real result without facing a big crowd.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel seeing Trisha read now?
qa.a: Deepika may feel glad that last year's quick no was not the final answer, and pleased that the small circle gave Trisha somewhere to start.

grounding: Shows an adult who rates a fear of reading aloud, tests it in a small circle, and keeps a record that makes Trisha's forecasts kinder.

passage:
Supervisor's note, city library, children's section

Elizabeth joined us in March and has been sure she cannot lead Saturday storytime. "The children will get bored and start running around," she said. "I'm ninety percent sure."

I asked her to write that number down, then try a small version: ten minutes, one picture book, five children, with me in the room. Afterwards she wrote what actually happened: "Two wriggled. One asked for the book again. Nobody ran."

We've kept this up for six weeks. Every Saturday she writes her forecast and her confidence before, and what happened after. Her first forecasts were all ninety or above for disaster. Last week she wrote, "Some will lose focus by the end. Sixty percent." And that is roughly what happened, which she laughed about.

The record seems to be making her guesses more accurate, and much less harsh on herself.

Next step: next month she'll lead the full thirty minutes, and I'll sit at the back.

— Anjali

qa.q: What did Elizabeth write after the first small storytime?
qa.a: "Two wriggled. One asked for the book again. Nobody ran."

qa.q: Why might Elizabeth have laughed about last week's forecast?
qa.a: She had predicted some children would lose focus and it happened roughly as she'd said, so she could see her guesses becoming realistic. It was probably a relief to be right about something that wasn't a disaster.

qa.q: What makes the small-version experiment work better than just telling Elizabeth she'll be fine?
qa.a: Elizabeth collects her own evidence each week by writing the forecast, trying a small version and recording what happened. Over time the record, not reassurance, corrects her predictions.

qa.q: How might the children at storytime experience Elizabeth's changing confidence?
qa.a: The children probably notice a calmer, more relaxed reader as the weeks pass. A reader who expects things to go all right may also be more playful with them.

grounding: A supervisor records how a young woman who predicted failure rated her confidence, tried small versions and compared results, so her forecasts became more accurate and kinder.

passage:
Thursday, Bengaluru. Entry 9 in the prediction notebook.

Vijay started this for me three weeks ago when I refused to try Kannada at the vegetable market. My forecast then: "They'll laugh, I'll freeze, I'll go home with nothing. 95% sure."

Today's plan was small: ask the tomato lady the price in Kannada. Only that.

Before: 80% sure it'll go badly.

What happened: I got one word wrong. She corrected me, smiling, and then told me her daughter is learning Hindi and mixes things up too. I bought tomatoes and coriander. She threw in two green chillies free.

So: forecast wrong again.

Looking back through the notebook, my numbers are coming down on their own. Entry 1 was 95. Entry 5 was 70. Today, 80, and it still went fine. I'm not saying I'm brave now. But the notebook knows more about me than my fear does.

Tomorrow: ask the bus conductor something.

Preeti

qa.q: What did the tomato lady throw in free?
qa.a: She threw in two green chillies free.

qa.q: What does Preeti mean by "the notebook knows more about me than my fear does"?
qa.a: Preeti feels the written record of what actually happened is more trustworthy than the fear, which keeps predicting disaster. The notebook shows a pattern the fear ignores.

qa.q: What small step would you suggest after the bus conductor?
qa.a: Keep raising the challenge a little, like a longer chat at the market, and keep writing the forecast and the result. The record will keep correcting the predictions.

qa.q: How might the tomato lady see Preeti's attempt at Kannada?
qa.a: She seemed pleased and warm, correcting gently and sharing that her own daughter mixes things up too. To her, the effort probably mattered more than the wrong word.

grounding: A young adult who predicts failure speaking Kannada keeps a notebook of forecasts and results, and the record makes the predictions kinder and more accurate.

passage: Charu had wanted to sell her mango pickle in the family's general store in Sinnar for a year, and every time she decided nobody would buy it. 'People here make their own,' she told her brother Saurabh. 'I'll be stuck with jars till Diwali.' This time Saurabh handed her the notebook they used for credit accounts. 'Write it. How sure are you?' On a fresh page she wrote: Nobody buys. 90% sure. Then she made only ten jars and put them by the counter, next to the matchboxes, with a handwritten card. By Sunday evening seven jars were gone, two to the schoolteacher, who said her own mother's recipe had been lost. Charu wrote under her prediction: 7 of 10. Wrong. Below it she started a new line for lime pickle: Maybe half sell. 60% sure.

qa.q: How many jars did Charu make for the test?
qa.a: Charu made only ten jars.

qa.q: Why did 'nobody will buy it' feel true to Charu for a whole year?
qa.a: She was afraid of being stuck with unsold jars and looking foolish, so the gloomy forecast felt safer and more certain than hope.

qa.q: What made Charu's experiment a good countermeasure?
qa.a: She wrote a prediction with a confidence level, tried a small version of ten jars and compared the result, so her next forecast for lime pickle was more realistic.

qa.q: What is it like for Saurabh to see the notebook page on Sunday?
qa.a: Saurabh would likely feel pleased that his push to write it down paid off, and glad to see his sister's forecasts growing more hopeful.

grounding: A young woman who predicts failure rates her confidence, tries a small batch and compares the result, making her next forecast more accurate.

passage: Anders had been saying for months that a board-game evening at his flat in Aarhus would be a disaster. 'No one will come, or they'll come and be bored and leave by nine,' he told Yosef over lunch. Yosef, who had a habit of writing things on napkins, pushed one across the table. 'Put a number on it. How sure?' 'Ninety percent.' 'Then try a small one. Three people, one game, Thursday.' Anders invited three colleagues from the warehouse. Two came, and one brought her sister. They played a card game and argued cheerfully about the rules until half past ten. Afterwards Anders pulled the napkin out of his jacket and wrote beside the ninety: 'Wrong. Next time: maybe 50% someone gets bored. Still worth it.' He had kept three napkins like that since spring, and each number was smaller than the last.

qa.q: Why had Anders put off the evening for months?

qa.q: Which choice turned the prediction into something testable?

qa.q: How might Yosef feel reading the napkin notes?
qa.a: Yosef would likely feel glad and amused to see the numbers shrinking, proof that one small nudge helped the forecasts grow kinder.

passage:
At the district hospital, Sarita was asked to lead the Tuesday talk for new mothers on the ward. Her stomach dropped. I'll forget everything, they'll get bored, I'll stumble over every word. In her notebook she wrote: Prediction: disaster. Confidence it goes badly: 90 percent.

Nirmala, the senior sister, didn't argue. "Try a small version first. Five minutes, three mothers, just the part about sleep routines. Then write what really happened."

On Monday Sarita spoke to three mothers for five minutes. She forgot one point. One mother asked a question she could answer. Nobody looked bored. She wrote: Actual: mostly fine. One forgotten point.

On Tuesday, before the full talk, she wrote a new prediction: Might forget things, 50 percent. It went well enough. She kept the notebook, and each week her numbers crept closer to what actually happened.

qa.q: How many mothers did Sarita speak to on Monday?
qa.a: Sarita spoke to three mothers.

qa.q: How did Sarita feel when first asked to lead the talk?
qa.a: Sarita felt anxious, her stomach dropping, and was 90 percent sure it would be a disaster.

qa.q: Why did the small version and the notebook help?
qa.a: Trying five minutes first and comparing prediction with result gave real evidence, so her next forecast was kinder and more accurate.

qa.q: How might the three mothers have experienced Sarita's short talk?
qa.a: They seemed engaged, asking a question and not looking bored, unaware of how nervous Sarita was.

grounding: Shows a young nurse who rates her fear of failing, tries a small version, and compares the result with her forecast.

passage:
Dear Aparna,

Remember I told you I'd never drive on the highway? That I'd panic, freeze, cause an accident? I rated it 95 percent certain. So for two years I only drove to the market and back.

Last month I tried your idea. Not the highway. A small version: the ring road on a Sunday morning, with my cousin beside me. Before, I wrote: "Prediction: I'll panic and pull over. 80 percent." After, I wrote: "Actual: sweaty hands for ten minutes, then okay. Didn't pull over."

Two Sundays later, a longer stretch. Prediction: 60 percent. Actual: fine, even enjoyed a song on the radio.

The notebook is funny now. Every prediction is worse than what happened. I'm starting to trust my forecasts less and my experiments more.

Next month, the highway to Mysuru, with you in the passenger seat?

Manjula

qa.q: Where did Manjula first drive as a small version?
qa.a: Manjula drove the ring road on a Sunday morning, with a cousin alongside.

qa.q: How did Manjula feel on the first ring-road drive?
qa.a: Manjula felt nervous, with sweaty hands for ten minutes, and then okay.

qa.q: Why is Manjula's notebook useful?
qa.a: Comparing each prediction with the actual result shows the forecasts are too gloomy, so Manjula's predictions become more accurate and kinder.

qa.q: How might Aparna feel being asked to sit in the passenger seat?
qa.a: Aparna would likely feel pleased and proud of Manjula, glad that the idea worked.

grounding: A letter shows an adult who rated a fear of highway driving, tried small drives, and compared each forecast with the result.

Imran, you asked why I finally started the poetry evenings. So. I'm Yusuf, and for years I told myself nobody would come. I'd set up chairs, and it would be me, the chairs, and maybe my mother out of pity. I'd have given it 95 percent.

Then a friend said, "Test it small." So I didn't book a hall. I posted in our building group: "Reading three poems on the terrace, Sunday, 6 pm, bring tea." I wrote my forecast on my phone first: "Two people, maybe."

Eleven came. Eleven! Mrs Fernandes brought pakoras.

I wrote: "Forecast: two. Actual: eleven." Next month I forecast eight. Fourteen came. Now I keep a little table: guess, then real. My guesses are still too gloomy, but they're getting closer. And kinder.

qa.q: How many people came to the first terrace reading?
qa.a: Eleven people came.

qa.q: Why did Yusuf predict only two people?
qa.a: Yusuf felt anxious about being embarrassed and alone, and years of gloomy forecasts made emptiness feel certain.

qa.q: What makes the table of guesses and real numbers useful?
qa.a: It gives Yusuf fresh evidence each month, so the forecasts become more accurate and less harsh.

qa.q: How might Mrs Fernandes have experienced the terrace evening?
qa.a: Mrs Fernandes probably enjoyed it enough to bring pakoras, happy to share tea and poems with neighbours.

passage: I'm Seema, and I've shared a flat with Kalyani for two years. She has always said, "I'd make a fool of myself," about speaking at her office's monthly meetings. In March I saw her doing something new. She had a small notebook. On one page she wrote: "Say one idea at Friday meeting. Prediction: they'll ignore me. Confidence: 80%." I didn't ask about it, but on Friday evening she came home and wrote under it: "Manager said 'good point', and Anil asked a follow-up." Next week: "Present one slide. Prediction: I'll stumble. Confidence: 70%." Result: "Stumbled once, nobody noticed." I don't know what goes on in her head, but I could see the confidence numbers dropping, page by page. By June she was volunteering for the quarterly presentation. When I teased her about the notebook, she just said, "My predictions were lying to me."

qa.q: What did Kalyani write as her first prediction?
qa.a: "Prediction: they'll ignore me. Confidence: 80%."

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when she first started the notebook?
qa.a: Kalyani seems to have been nervous about speaking up, sure of looking foolish, yet hopeful enough to test it.

qa.q: Why does the notebook work?
qa.a: Each small try is compared with the written forecast, so over time the record shows the predictions were too gloomy and they become more accurate.

qa.q: How might Seema feel watching Kalyani volunteer by June?
qa.a: Seema seems quietly impressed and pleased, having watched the confidence numbers drop page by page.

grounding: A flatmate observes an adult who predicts failure rating her confidence, trying small steps and comparing results until her predictions become kinder.

Monday. Shankar had wanted to ask his manager for one work-from-home day a week for months, to help his mother after her knee operation. "She'll say no and think I'm lazy," he told Elizabeth, his colleague. Elizabeth handed him a sticky note. "Write the prediction and how sure you are." He wrote: "No. 85%."
Wednesday. Shankar asked for just one trial day, not every week. The manager said, "Try Friday, let's see how it goes." He came back to Elizabeth, stunned. On the sticky note, he wrote: "Result: yes to a trial."
The next Friday. The trial had gone fine. Shankar asked for a regular Friday. "Prediction: no. 60%." The answer was yes. He stuck both notes inside his drawer. "Look at that," Elizabeth said. "Eighty-five, then sixty. Your forecasts are getting kinder." Shankar grinned. "They're getting more accurate."

qa.q: What did Shankar write on the first sticky note?
qa.a: He wrote: "No. 85%."

qa.q: How did Shankar feel when the manager said yes to a trial?
qa.a: Shankar was stunned and relieved, because his prediction had been a confident no.

qa.q: Why did asking for one trial day work well as a first step?
qa.a: It was a small, safe version of the request, so the result could be compared with his forecast before asking for more.

qa.q: What might Elizabeth notice as she watches the sticky notes?
qa.a: Elizabeth can see Shankar's confidence in failure dropping, and seems pleased to watch his forecasts become kinder.

grounding: Over two weeks an adult who predicts rejection rates his confidence, tests a small request, and compares results so his forecasts become more accurate.

passage: Nandini, you think your paintings won't sell, so you won't try the craft fair? Sit. Your Vaibhav Kaka will tell you about the lamps. When I was twenty-four I made clay lamps in the shed behind our house in Nashik. I was certain nobody would buy them. "Too plain," I'd say. "People want shiny things." My friend Aruna said, "Stop saying it. Test it." So I took just five lamps to the Sunday market. Before I left, I wrote on a scrap of paper: "Sell zero. Sure: 90%." I sold three. Next week I took ten and wrote: "Sell two. Sure: 60%." I sold seven. I kept those scraps in a biscuit tin. After a year my guesses were almost right every time, and they had become much kinder. So take five paintings, beti. Write your guess. Then see.

qa.q: How many lamps did Vaibhav take to the Sunday market the first time?
qa.a: Vaibhav took just five lamps.

qa.q: How did young Vaibhav feel about the lamps before the first market?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt doubtful and discouraged, certain nobody would buy them because they were too plain.

qa.q: What choice in the story changed things for Vaibhav?
qa.a: Following Aruna's advice to test it, taking five lamps and writing down a prediction to compare with what really happened.

qa.q: How might Aruna have felt when Vaibhav sold three lamps?
qa.a: Aruna was probably pleased and not very surprised, having believed the prediction was just fear talking.

grounding: An uncle recalls testing his gloomy forecast about selling lamps with small tries, writing each guess down until his predictions grew accurate and kinder.

Sudha had wanted to sell her mango pickle for years, but a stall at the Sunday market cost money she couldn't spare, and she was sure no one would buy.
"Rate it," said her friend Bhavna, who kept a bangle stall there. "How sure are you that it flops?"
"Ninety percent."
"Then test it small. Put ten jars on my table this Sunday. Write your guess on the lid of the box."
Sudha wrote: "Maybe two jars sell."
It drizzled all morning, and the crowd was thin. By noon seven jars were gone, and a woman asked if she took orders. That evening Sudha opened a notebook and drew two columns, "Guessed" and "Happened". Under the first she wrote 2. Under the second, 7.
"Next time," she said, "I'll guess four."

qa.q: How many jars did Sudha guess would sell?

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling before the test?
qa.a: She felt doubtful and afraid, ninety percent sure the pickle would flop.

qa.q: Why is Sudha's two-column notebook a good habit?
qa.a: Comparing each guess with what actually happened makes her predictions more accurate and kinder over time 👍, like guessing four next time.

qa.q: How might Bhavna feel watching the jars sell?
